title: The endowment
hookLine: a property given forever for good: a well, a school, a hospital

lines: KEEP THE ROOT, GIVE THE FRUIT.
cards: Umar ibn al-Khattab had come into a piece of land at Khaybar, and, as he put it, he had never owned anything he valued more. He went to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and asked what to do with it.
The answer, reported in Sahih al-Bukhari, comes to this: if you wish, keep the land itself, and give away what it produces. So Umar did. The land could not be sold, given or inherited.
Its harvest went to the poor, to relatives, to freeing slaves, to the cause of God, to travelers and to guests. Keep the root. Give the fruit.
A new part of the path begins: institutions. Today: the endowment.

teach.h: A GIFT BUILT NOT TO END.
teach.b: The word is waqf: property set aside so it can never be sold, with its income given for good, on and on.
You've met waqf at work on this path already: the hospitals that sent no bill, the colleges where students got a room and bread. Here's the idea underneath. A gift usually ends.
You give a meal, and it's eaten. A waqf is built not to end.
A row of shops is endowed, and their rent pays a teacher. A farm is endowed, and its grain feeds the hungry. The giver dies.
The shops are still rented. The teacher is still paid. Why give this way?

A saying of the Prophet in Sahih Muslim says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge that brings benefit, and a righteous child who prays for them.
Ongoing charity, sadaqah jariyah, charity that keeps flowing. A waqf is that hadith set in stone and soil.

teach.h: SPEND OF THAT WHICH YE LOVE.
teach.b: And the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "Ye will not attain unto piety until ye spend of that which ye love." Umar gave the land he valued most. Sultans endowed mosques and hospitals.
Ordinary people, women and men, endowed a fountain, a shelf of books, a bed in a hospital. Some waqfs fed people long after their founders died.
Others were mismanaged, seized, or simply forgotten; forever is a hard promise for human hands to keep. Today some Muslims are reviving the idea, with endowed wells, scholarships and funds.

how: Muslims still found waqfs for mosques, schools, wells and scholarships, often through charities that manage the endowment and spend only its income, and speak of it as sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity.

games.q: you're Umar. you hold the most valuable land you've ever owned, and you ask the Prophet what to do. what does he suggest?
o: sell it and give the money away at once.
keep the land itself and give away what it produces.
keep it all for your family.
games.why: keep the root, give the fruit. the land could not be sold, given or inherited; its harvest went to the poor, relatives, travelers and guests.

practice: Bring to mind something good you'd love to see still running after you're gone, a library, a scholarship, a clean-water project, a habit you teach a child, and settle on the smallest real step toward it: a small recurring gift, a skill to teach, a name to look up.
If you pray, you can ask that it outlast you.
